boulder/2023-06-22_01aYfhQ1J-s: The city announced that the 2023 boards and commissions recruitment period is open through July 2, with eight boards accepting applications. Clerk Elisha Johnson took roll and a quorum was confirmed.

The council voted unanimously to add a declaration honoring Judge Cook, an introduction of Ordinance 8583 imposing a moratorium on the police oversight panel, and appointment of two ad hoc liaisons to the Better Public Meetings project. The amended agenda passed.

Council read a declaration recognizing Judge Cook's 22 years with the Boulder Municipal Court, including restorative justice partnerships with CU Boulder and the homeless Navigator and community court programs. Judge Cook thanked the council and colleagues. Council members praised her leadership and said she would be missed.

Sarah Huntley described the Better Public Meetings pilot with the National Civic League, which will review official council meetings. Staff recommended appointing Matt Benjamin and Rachel Friend as ad hoc liaisons. Both agreed to serve.

Council members Yates and Wallach opposed a council-imposed moratorium on new police oversight panel cases, arguing it sets a precedent that boards can stop work without consequence. Staff said the panel did not request the moratorium but several members welcomed it, and that a special counsel might be needed for a code of conduct complaint. Council discussed timing for the ordinance revisions and the October 20 end date. Council approved the consent agenda, including item 2B, with Wallach and Yates voting no on the moratorium.

Bob Yates asked about the process for filling the municipal judge position after Judge Cook retires. Judge Khan was introduced in person and thanked council for her appointment as interim successor. Council welcomed her to the role.

Staff presented second reading of Ordinance 8577 rezoning about 1.01 acres from Industrial General to Business Community, consistent with the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan and Gun Barrel Community Center plan. The planning board recommended approval 6-0 and staff received no public comment. One resident spoke in opposition, favoring retaining industrial space. Council unanimously adopted the ordinance.

Judge Cook and lead Navigator Nia Nguyen described the court's community court program, which uses outreach and navigators to connect high-acuity unhoused clients to services, housing, and court-ordered alternatives. Data showed most clients refuse shelter and many are impaired, but alternative sanctions have increased accountability compared with 2019. Council members thanked Judge Cook for her work and her impact on the community.

County Clerk Molly Fitzpatrick reviewed voter registration trends and the 2023 coordinated election timeline, plus four back-to-back elections beginning this fall. She outlined implementation of ranked choice voting for Boulder's mayoral race, including voting system upgrades, voter education, and Spanish-language materials. Council members asked about how rounds will be reported, ballot length limits, adjudication rates, and surveys after the election.

The city clerk certified two citizen initiative petitions, the Safe Zones for Kids petition and an arts, culture, and heritage sales tax extension, both with enough valid signatures. Staff are polling voters on extending the expiring 0.15 percent sales and use tax, with results expected before a July 20 first reading. Council is considering a 20-year extension versus no sunset, and a charter cleanup initiative is being drafted.

Staff reviewed a potential tax on tobacco, liquor, and an added marijuana increment, with revenue estimates. Proposed uses include on-site clinicians and prescriber services at the planned homeless services day center, a high utilizer team proposal, and capital support for Mental Health Partners acute care expansion. Council will receive more information on the high utilizer plan in August, and the tax was not placed on the November ballot.

Josh Hanson introduced the 2024 Boulder energy conservation code development project aimed at meeting 2030 and 2035 carbon reduction goals. Proposed updates include revised energy use intensity targets for commercial buildings and a Zero Energy Ready home pathway for residential projects. Staff sought feedback on areas of focus and community engagement, with a first public reading targeted for Q4 2023.

Staff proposed requiring all-electric space and water heating for new construction and major alterations, with electric-ready requirements for other appliances. EV charging requirements would be strengthened, including for smaller lots and e-bikes, and natural gas uses would require full offsets through renewables. Council members supported moving toward all-electric requirements, and a straw poll showed majority interest.

Staff discussed reducing embodied carbon through life cycle assessments and material choices, and considering mass timber as a lower-carbon building option. Council members encouraged aligning energy code updates with zoning changes to make retrofits easier and asked how the code would affect affordability for lower-cost homes. Staff said incentives and community engagement, including with frontline climate-impacted residents, would be considered.
boulder/2023-07-13_K3Nkg5ubIUU: Council recognized July as Parks and Recreation Month, and Parks and Recreation staff reflected on departmental achievements, including record free-access program visits and upcoming projects such as Violet Park. Council thanked staff for their work. No vote was required beyond the agenda amendment.
Council approved the consent agenda, consisting of items 2A through 2C, by unanimous voice vote after a motion and second.

Council held a public hearing to review and comment on the Boulder Valley School District's site development plan to replace New Vista High School with a roughly 74,000 square foot two-story building, new sports field, and reconfigured parking and access. Staff explained the review is per state statute and no approval or denial was taken. The district presented changes made since May, including 18 fewer parking spaces, 64 bike stalls, added EV charging, a sidewalk link, and a revised athletic field approach. Council members praised the responsiveness, asked about construction waste, cross-laminated timber, geothermal grants, and an accessible multi-use path from the east, and a resident urged the project proceed quickly.

Council reviewed a concept plan for a roughly 107,250 square foot mixed-use North Boulder Creative Campus including a new Boulder Museum of Contemporary Art, 67 residential units, retail, and studio space, requiring a 29-space parking reduction and several code modifications. Staff explained the museum use is prohibited in the MU-2 zone and live-work units are prohibited in RM-1, so rezoning, a North Boulder subcommunity plan update, and likely a flex zone would be needed. Council members were generally supportive of the museum use, the land use change path, and the project's consistency with comprehensive plan goals, and asked the applicant to address liquor licensing near the school, the land donation value, and displacement of existing tenants. Council also discussed a possible referral to the Design Advisory Board and Transportation Advisory Board, with the applicant to decide timing, and asked that bike and pedestrian safety be coordinated with Community Cycles.

Staff presented polling by Probolsky Research showing about 70 percent support for extending the 0.15 percent sales tax, with a 62 percent approval rating for city services. Council discussed a compromise proposed by petitioners of the arts ballot measure to split the 0.15 percent tax 50/50 between arts and the general fund, which would roughly double arts funding. Members debated the trade-offs, the dedicated-funds concern, the 1.8 million dollar existing arts allocation, and legal options. Seven members directed staff to prepare a 50/50 alternative ballot measure for next week, and staff was asked to conduct outreach to bipoc and lower-income arts organizations before final decisions.

Staff reported that 12 applications were received for 12 vacancies, with several boards receiving no eligible applicants and interviews completed by council members. Council discussed whether applicants could be placed on other boards and whether the recruitment should be extended. A majority of council, seven members, directed staff to defer unfilled vacancies to the 2024 annual recruitment, which will be prepared beginning in September 2023.
boulder/2023-07-20_FLEm6gGcS-M: Residents, representatives of public health groups, and industry advocates spoke during open comment. Public health speakers urged the Council to keep smoke-free air protections and opposed allowing smoking or vaping in public places, including cannabis. Chamber of Commerce and cannabis industry speakers supported marijuana hospitality establishments as a way to regulate consumption and support business. Several speakers also raised concerns about drug harm reduction services and public drug use downtown.

Union members and residents urged the Council to join Boulder County in raising the local minimum wage, with some asking for implementation in 2024 rather than 2025. Speakers framed the wage increase as an economic security and housing affordability measure. The Chamber of Commerce asked for a deliberate process that accounts for small nonprofit budgets. A staff update later noted that nearby communities preferred 2025 implementation.

The Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3H unanimously. The agenda included three alternative versions of a ballot measure to extend the 0.15 percent sales tax that would otherwise expire at the end of next year. Council planned to pass all three on first reading and hold a public hearing on August 3 before narrowing the options. Another consent item allowed land use approvals to remain valid for three years instead of one.

Staff presented Cannabis Licensing Advisory Board recommendations on opting in to state law allowing marijuana hospitality establishments. Staff asked whether Council wanted this added to a future work plan and what level of public engagement to pursue. Most Council members said the item should not be added this year because of staff capacity and the timing near the end of the term. Council opted not to direct a consultant or engagement now and suggested the next Council consider the item at its retreat.

Fire Chief Calderazzo and Parks and Recreation Director Rhodes described emergency response to recent Boulder Creek drownings and current closure protocols tied to county flow thresholds of 700 cubic feet per second. Proposed measures include throw-line stations, temporary and permanent signage by April 2024, and a Creek Management Plan. Council discussed requiring personal flotation devices, expanding swim lessons through financial aid, and coordinating with the sheriff and the school district. Council members expressed condolences to the families affected.
boulder/2023-07-27_BjtqgUm0b5g: City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde introduced consultant Farah Muscadin, former Austin oversight director, who presented preliminary observations and a timeline for revising the police oversight ordinance. Her recommendations included removing the independent monitor from the panel as a non-voting member, formalizing onboarding and training within 90 days, and using standard operating procedures for details better suited than ordinance text. Council members asked about ordinance drafting versus implementation, the term oversight, the panel's size, and monitor hiring. Council discussed the ambiguous perceived bias criterion and how the panel's discipline recommendation process should work.

Council members thanked Farah and the working group and asked for further attention to training development, a grievance process for disagreements over discipline, and a regular cadence for revisiting the ordinance. Questions about outside counsel led staff to explain that the City Attorney's Office represents all boards and commissions and would hire outside counsel only for significant conflicts. Council asked for a survey of how other cities structure their panels.

Planner Lisa Hood presented the third and final use table module, focused on neighborhood centers in business, downtown, and mixed-use zones, to implement Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan policies on walkable 15-minute neighborhoods. Residential zoning changes were deferred to the future comprehensive plan update. Staff summarized community engagement through a story map, questionnaire (about 190 responses by early July, closing July 31), pop-ups, and working group input. Public input favored more restaurants, small grocery stores, and local retail while expressing concern about auto-oriented uses.

Staff explained that 12 different restaurant regulations across zones make most restaurants require use review, and proposed raising by-right size thresholds, easing patio size limits, and allowing by-right restaurants in downtown zones. Council members broadly supported simplifying approvals and making Boulder a top place to open a restaurant, with suggestions to extend changes to the Hill and to consider limits on chain restaurants. Staff said the City Attorney would investigate chain restaurant distinctions. Staff noted that revenue is cost recovery and that administrative oversight would remain.

Staff proposed allowing duplexes and townhomes on ground floors by right in BT and BR zones, which currently require use review, while keeping BC retail cores unchanged. Council members were divided: some supported middle housing and transition to residential areas, while others worried about displacing retail, density compatibility, and equity and mixed-income concerns. Staff said it had enough direction to move forward and that the questionnaire would provide additional input.

Staff proposed prohibiting car washes, drive-throughs, fuel service stations, and fuel sales in downtown zoning districts to support walkability, noting few such uses currently exist downtown and that proposals would still need use review criteria. Council members raised concerns about accessibility for people with mobility limits, pharmacy and food drive-throughs, convenience stores serving food deserts, EV charging, and whether prohibition was needed. Many members preferred retaining review rather than outright prohibition.

Staff presented additional proposed changes to allow government facilities such as post offices, small retail in mixed-use zones, small-scale medical offices and repair services, small theaters or music venues, and temporary events in mixed-use zones, while reviewing museums, lodges, hostels, and animal hospitals more carefully. Council generally supported the changes, especially retail and post offices, though members asked for more information about hostels and lodges and cautioned about noise and compatibility for performance spaces. Members also urged reimagining older neighborhood centers and consideration of small arts spaces.
boulder/2023-08-03_ldO17Yp3jiM: The Council voted unanimously to amend the agenda to add a birthday tribute for Councilmember Tara Leonard. Roll call was then taken for the meeting.

Council Member Yates presented a declaration recognizing August and September 2023 as a time to celebrate pollinators and little creatures. Staff described the library gallery exhibit and the Boulder Festival on September 9th. Local children joined the Council to help read the declaration.

Residents spoke on a proposed homeless daycare center on Folsom Street, camping and sweeps, historic preservation of the Civic Area park, the Saddle Creek wall, and mental health and jail concerns. Other speakers addressed minimum wage, bus service, lease paperwork at Boulder Housing Partners, and occupancy limits. Staff and Council responded by noting upcoming study sessions and referring issues to RTD and the County.

The Council approved the consent agenda items A through E with a motion and second. Item 3B, the occupancy ordinance on first reading, received no votes from Councilmembers Weiner and Yates and Mayor Pro Tem Wallach. Councilmember Friend disclosed a short-term rental license and chose not to recuse. The public hearing on occupancy is scheduled for August 17.

The Council held a public hearing on second reading of Ordinance 8580 to designate 830 14th Street as the Powers House, an individual landmark within the University Place historic district. Staff described the 1920 Craftsman Bungalow and its associations with Kate and Patrick Powers. One speaker questioned the Landmarks Board process and the demolition of nearby historic homes. The Council adopted the ordinance unanimously.

Staff presented Ordinance 8586, the Safe Zones for Kids petition, which would prioritize removal of prohibited items near schools and multi-use paths. Staff also presented Ordinance 8587, which would amend Charter sections on election procedures and petition signature requirements. Both items were continued to August 17 for final action, with a public hearing held at that time.

Staff explained the expiring 0.15 percent sales and use tax and the three competing ordinances: the Arts for Boulder petition (8589), the staff proposal (8588), and the compromise (8591). The compromise would split revenue 50 percent to the general fund and 50 percent to arts, culture, and heritage programs. Finance staff said the compromise would not force direct cuts but would constrain future budget choices. Staff also noted that the library district funds have been tapped for other priorities.

Speakers, including Arts leaders and community members, supported the 50/50 compromise to benefit arts and general services. One speaker urged a 100 percent arts allocation, and others expressed concern about taxes and the cost of living. Several speakers emphasized the economic and social value of the arts to Boulder. Staff indicated that the arts petition had consensus among Arts leaders for the compromise.

Council members debated whether to keep all three ballot options or pick only the compromise, weighing voter choice against long-term financial goals. Councilmember Benjamin moved and Councilmember Yates seconded to pass and amend Ordinance 8591, the 50/50 compromise, which passed seven to two. Councilmember Yates then moved to pass Ordinance 8589 as amended, which passed nine to zero. Ordinance 8588 was not voted on and will return on August 17.

Staff updated Council on the 311 Mapleton development, where the original inclusionary housing agreement lapsed and the developer paid cash in lieu. The new voluntary agreement has the developer donate the Fruehauf site and pay $1.7 million in cash, worth about $8 million total compared with the roughly $3.8 million legally required. Closing is expected the week of August 17, and the site will go to Boulder Housing Partners for affordable senior housing. Council praised staff for securing a better outcome and asked that future processes avoid similar delays.

Staff responded to a Council request on the external evaluation of homelessness services, which is being scoped jointly with Boulder County with an RFP expected in September and award in December. Staff also reported research on safe outdoor camping models from Madison, Louisville, and Portland. Council gave direction to modify the RFP to include a city-specific examination of gaps and safe outdoor space options. Council asked for a scheduling update and an information item on whether safe outdoor spaces could be added to the work plan before the September study session.
boulder/2023-08-10_LXeTm-84ZtQ: The city clerk outlined vacancies on the Environmental Advisory Board, Landmarks Board, Open Space Board of Trustees, and University Hill Commercial Area Management Commission. No one signed up to speak during the public hearing, which was closed. Council nominated and voted on candidates using the finalist process, with the rounds producing Hannah Davis, Greg Hill, Renee Golbeck, Harmon Zuckerman, and Tell Jones as appointees. Council then unanimously approved the slate.

Staff presented history, regulations, safety concerns, a 14 percent commercial vacancy rate, and funding constraints for the University Hill General Improvement District. Recommendations included district identity work, improved connectivity along 13th Street, and activation efforts, with staff proposing to prioritize these before redeveloping the 14th Street lot. Council asked questions about the liquor rules, parking, and the Hill Hotel's impact, and members generally supported the broad strategies and exploring code changes.

Staff and CU Real Estate Center graduate students presented research on rising commercial lease costs in Boulder and peer programs in other cities. The proposal is a five-year pilot in which the city would master-lease space and sublease to small businesses and nonprofits at reduced operating costs, paired with free education, with a program administrator selected through an RFP. Council members raised questions about eligibility, sustainability, funding sources, and cost to the city, and generally supported continuing the exploration.
boulder/2023-08-17_zA5JVdBVOQk: Audit subcommittee member David Gross presented the 2022 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and the audit by Clifton Larson Allen. The auditor issued a clean opinion with no significant deficiencies or material weaknesses, the 33rd consecutive year of the GFOA certificate of achievement. Council members thanked the audit committee and finance staff, and the council later approved the report on the consent agenda.

Many residents, union members, and labor advocates urged the council to raise the local minimum wage to 15 dollars or more immediately rather than waiting until 2025. Speakers also raised concerns about airport noise, Human Services funding, the 0.15 percent sales tax, and a proposed mental health center. Staff committed to follow up on local business wage data and confirmed the city is still enforcing the camping ban.

Council asked staff whether the existing 0.15 percent tax is dedicated to any purpose and whether a 50/50 compromise measure must be placed on the ballot if the council does not act. Deputy City Attorney Aaron Poe confirmed the petitioners' 100 percent arts measure would proceed to the ballot unless withdrawn. Council also discussed Human Services funding concerns and the timing of the ballot deadline.

Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3I unanimously after Councilmember Benjamin pulled item 3J for separate discussion. Item 3H was an annexation for which a council member disclosed prior work with the property owners but still considered themselves impartial. Deputy City Attorney Aaron Poe then summarized the status of the five ballot measure ordinances, including the staff-recommended changes to the 50/50 compromise ordinance 8591.

Budget Officer Mark Wolfe explained that the 2024 recommended budget was built assuming renewal of the 0.15 percent tax, and that a half-dedicated option still avoids service cuts while a full general fund option offers the most flexibility. Council adopted ordinance 8586 and ordinance 8587 unanimously and defeated ordinance 8588, which would dedicate 100 percent to arts, by a vote of five to two to four. Council then approved the 50/50 compromise ordinance 8591 by a vote of six to three.

Staff presented a request to vacate a 14-foot-wide utility easement at 2950 Hawthorne Avenue, formerly 3320 28th Street, under case ADR 2023-00109. No council member asked to call up the item, so it proceeded without further review.

Planning staff presented Ordinance 8585, which would raise the citywide limit for unrelated occupants from three to five and change the limit for efficiency units to three. Staff described the project history, national comparisons, and community engagement results, including the 2,000 BeHeardBoulder responses that favored four more than five. The presentation also covered a proposed freeze on occupancy increases in non-conforming uses, with an option to limit it to university-adjacent zones, and the Planning Board's 4-3 recommendation of approval.

Dozens of residents, students, co-op members, and housing advocates spoke in favor of raising the occupancy limit, citing affordability, chosen families, and the need for shared housing. Opponents, including many Martin Acres and Hill residents, raised concerns about noise, parking, trash, enforcement, the 2021 bedrooms-for-people vote, and the lack of rent guarantees. Several speakers also asked for affordability requirements, stronger code enforcement, and attention to climate and traffic impacts.

Councilmember Rachel Friend moved to adopt Ordinance 8585, and a motion to remove the non-conforming use and occupancy provisions failed three to six. Council members who supported the change argued it would expand housing options, support students and chosen families, and that enforcement should target behaviors rather than people. Opponents said the change lacks affordability guarantees, overrides the 2021 vote, and could worsen neighborhood impacts, and the council then adopted Ordinance 8585 by a vote of six to three.
boulder/2023-08-24_YrPGGa7v3vE: Staff presented research on internet access and affordability, noting over 99 percent of households have wired broadband but only about 36 percent have fiber, with limited provider choice. Three potential paths were outlined: a municipal internet utility (estimated at $218 million, requiring about $268 million in debt and roughly $14 million annual general fund subsidy), a public-private partnership, and a non-exclusive backbone lease, which staff recommended as the lowest-risk and fastest option. Council asked follow-up questions on take rates, lease conditions, equity of build-out, and financing, and staff will return with more information at a future public hearing.

Staff presented results of community engagement on the future of the Boulder Municipal Airport, including questionnaires, open houses, and a community working group, and four draft scenarios ranging from enhanced maintenance to decommissioning and redeveloping the site. Community input emphasized noise, leaded fuel, and safety concerns, with near-term action items identified. Council discussed FAA grant assurances and closure obligations, with the FAA indicating closure would be difficult, and asked for more legal and factual clarity before returning in early 2024.

Staff updated council on the regional minimum wage working group with Longmont, Louisville, Lafayette, and Erie, and on Boulder County's decision to pursue a 15 percent increase effective January 2024. Staff noted that accelerating Boulder's timeline would require pausing regional collaboration and conducting a shorter engagement process without an economic analysis. Council members debated the tradeoffs between responding to urgent community need and maintaining regional partnership, and by a 5-4 vote directed staff to stay with the regional 2025 timeline.
boulder/2023-09-07_OvkYrrlrfw4: Council read declarations recognizing the 10th anniversary of the 2013 Front Range flood, National Voter Registration Day on September 19, and National Suicide Prevention Month. Rise Against Suicide's Jenna Carr and Lauren spoke in appreciation of the recognition. Staff also announced the What's Up Boulder event and the Better Public Meetings scorecard.

Residents spoke on the proposed Boulder Airport closure, police oversight and officer conduct, the hill commercial area liquor regulations, and bear activity and trash in the University Hill area. Other speakers raised South Boulder maintenance concerns and homelessness camp proposals. Council members and staff responded and committed to follow-ups.

Council approved the consent agenda items 3a through 3i unanimously. Item 3h concerned a planning matter with a second reading scheduled for September 21 and possible third reading. Item 3i was Resolution 1339 supporting LGBTQ+ people's access to goods, services, and public accommodations without discrimination in light of the 303 Creative decision.
Council considered calling up a site review for three student housing apartment buildings at 1345 28th Street. No member requested a call-up, so the item proceeded with planning board review.

Chief Maris Harold, Wendy Schwarz, and Robin Engel of the National Policing Institute presented the Reimagine Policing Plan, which emphasizes problem-solving policing, holistic governance, staffing aligned to the ICMA rule of 60, and accountability metrics. Staff noted that the funding requests would come through future budget cycles. Council and speakers largely supported the plan, though some residents raised concerns about downtown crime and staffing levels.

Speakers representing business groups, neighborhood associations, and residents voiced strong support for the plan, citing crime on Pearl Street and in the downtown area. Some speakers called for more police staffing and criticized council decisions and the police oversight panel. Others urged equity and community engagement in implementation.

Council members praised the community engagement process and the work of the subcommittee. Several members stressed that the plan is a roadmap requiring ongoing implementation and accountability. Council then approved a motion to accept the plan and disband the subcommittee by roll call vote, unanimously.

Staff presented proposed updates to the inclusionary housing program, including moving cash-in-lieu to a per-square-foot basis, reducing the on-site for-sale requirement from 25% to 15%, and exploring a Nexus study for a linkage fee on demolitions and large additions. Kaiser Marston's feasibility analysis found developers consistently choose cash-in-lieu over on-site units. Council members expressed concern about trading on-site middle-income units for more off-site rental units, but supported the code cleanups and continued analysis.
boulder/2023-09-14_hOn-ecXbgHw: Staff reviewed the history of forming the Boulder Public Library District, including the 2018 library master plan and the 2022 voter-approved district formation. Staff noted that the city will no longer treat library services as a core city function and that the district will be governed by its own trustees. Many transition issues such as IT and employment were described as technical, while appointment and property questions were flagged for council policy feedback.

Staff presented three options for selecting library trustees: continuing the joint council and county committee model, delegating selection to the trustees, or a hybrid with non-voting trustee participation. Council discussed reviewing the approach in three years, which aligned with staff's recommendation. Council members then gave a unanimous straw poll favoring the hybrid approach with a three-year check-in.

Staff outlined options for city-owned library buildings, including conveyance, leases, or a mix where the city keeps the land at the main library. Council straw polls favored leasing the branch libraries over transferring them, and the city also discussed a right of reversion. Members debated lease length, with trustees preferring a long-term lease, and eventually supported a 20 to 30 year lease with a district-only termination option at five-year intervals. Staff were directed to offer this as a possible negotiation point rather than a requirement.

The city manager and CFO introduced the $514.8 million 2024 recommended budget, emphasizing constrained resources and sustainability, equity, and resilience goals. Staff projected sales and use tax about 2.3 percent lower than prior models, citing slowing retail and inflation. Property assessments rose about 32 percent, with Proposition HH on the November ballot and a possible property tax cap being monitored. The general fund includes a one-time $13 million repayment expected from the Library District.

Community connectors Jamal Gilmore and Lenora Cooper presented feedback gathered over several months from historically excluded communities. Top priorities included housing affordability, financial security and economic opportunity, and advancing racial equity. Mental health and youth opportunities emerged as the biggest shifts in community needs. Council thanked the connectors and expressed interest in continued partnership, one-on-one meetings, and expanded engagement in future budgets.

Staff highlighted major investments including behavioral health response programs, $31.8 million for affordable housing including the Ponderosa stabilization project, and wildfire mitigation grants. New investments also covered living wage increases and collective bargaining agreements for city employees. The six-year capital program totals about $900 million, with the Western City Campus project and debt service increases to fund it. Other capital projects include East Boulder Community Center retrofits, new fire stations, and Pearl Street Mall improvements.

Staff reviewed operating investments across goal areas such as environmental sustainability, livability, safety, healthy community, and economic vitality. Staff acknowledged about $30 million in general fund unfunded needs, including facility maintenance, affordable housing, fire master plan implementation, and parks maintenance. A citywide strategic plan and a long-term financial strategy were proposed to guide future prioritization.

Staff explained the review timeline, with council change requests due September 25 and a first reading on October 5. Councilmembers asked about snow and ice removal, pothole repairs, the South Boulder Rec Center, Pilot program evaluation, and unspent day services funds. Council emphasized that any requested additions must identify offsetting reductions to maintain a zero-sum budget. Councilmembers praised staff for the budget work and thanked the community connectors before the meeting closed at 9:50 pm.
boulder/2023-09-21_YWNAVc24Huk: Council presented a proclamation recognizing Hispanic Heritage Month from September 15 to October 15, with interpreters and community members speaking in Spanish and English. Council then presented an Energy Efficiency Day declaration for October 2023, urging residents to support clean energy goals.

Eight in-person speakers and one virtual speaker addressed Council on topics including library building disposition, a Museum of Boulder exhibit, police monitor and homelessness near Central Park, architectural preservation, potty training facilities, a Landmarks Design Review Committee demolition, and a 28th and J housing project. Staff responded to several concerns, including the Central Park incident and the housing project.
Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3F unanimously by roll call. No council member called up the Life Sciences site review at 3825 Walnut Street, so it proceeded without a call-up.

Staff presented amendments to the 2007 Transit Village Area Plan covering land use, transportation connections, and urban design for the Boulder Junction Phase 2 area. Council discussed mixed-use transit-oriented development versus mixed-use industrial zoning, anti-displacement strategies for small businesses, and retail sizing. Council approved both motions unanimously, including the staff recommendation not to add the planning board's office restriction.

Staff presented second reading amendments to the land use code to ease density, parking, and subdivision rules, aiming to increase middle housing and modest-size units. Council discussed site review exemptions, efficiency living unit use review, floor area bonuses, and rmx-1 rezoning, deferring several items to a future phase. Council amended and passed the ordinance unanimously, with a third reading expected as a consent item.

Council member Benjamin proposed a letter to County Commissioners endorsing a proposed affordable and attainable housing tax, requesting investment in permanent supportive housing with wraparound services and transitional housing. Council generally supported sending the letter, with a formal endorsement resolution to follow through a future request.
boulder/2023-09-28_twY2b6ioVSQ: Judge Conan described the court's problem-solving philosophy, administrative changes, and the new live-stream requirement. She explained the FastTrack process for student quality-of-life violations, which emphasizes quick court dates and restorative justice with CU. Council members questioned how prosecutors choose between Community Court and traditional court, and staff agreed to provide the eligibility criteria and a fuller explanation in a hotline post. Jail booking standards and the 48-hour PR bond rule were also discussed as constraints.

Council asked about longer jail sentences, which the judge said are rare and used only as a last resort after programs are refused. Questions addressed whether community court is reserved for unhoused people, and council requested data comparing outcomes and recidivism for those who use and do not use Community Court. Council members also asked about trespass charges, consequences, and the need for sober living and transitional housing after jail. A future conversation with the sheriff and prosecutor was requested.

Chief Harold presented five-year crime data showing rising simple and aggravated assaults and menacing, with robberies down and property theft up, while motor vehicle theft is down 48% since 2020. Drug and narcotics violations are up 79%, and downtown and University Hill account for a large share of overdoses and fatal overdoses, mostly involving fentanyl. Staff noted that officers are administering Narcan several times daily.

Deputy Chief Redfern reported on problem-location work at the library and the Circle K at 14th and Canyon, where directed patrols reduce crime when present. The department reviewed significant incidents including a fatal officer-involved shooting, a child homicide, a stolen-car standoff, two fatal motorcycle crashes with speed as a factor, a downtown stabbing with a released suspect, a Central Park drug operation, and a serious Hill burglary series. Council was told community outreach included Pride, a youth academy, an international policing conference, and K9 Astro's certification.

Council asked why jail capacity is strained, and staff said the jail is back at the pandemic-era cap of about 490 with a backlog of people awaiting competency trials. Discussion covered the impact of released defendants and an inability to hold people awaiting trial. Council asked how motor vehicle theft fell, and staff cited education, state investigators, stings and cameras. Council also raised concerns about hate crimes, domestic violence, human trafficking, drug combinations such as xylazine, and staffing needs, and staff agreed to send data.

Housing and Human Services presented a summer point-in-time count showing similar totals of about 350 single adults in winter and summer, and about 25 monthly exits from homelessness in Boulder. Staff described new programs including the local voucher program, shelter unit acquisitions, the Building Home program, a planned rest and recuperation center funded by a $2 million state grant, the High Utilizer partnership, and the Day Services Center, which lost its site but gained state funding for expanded services. The presentation also covered coordinated entry, racial equity data, the Outreach team, and a $11.6 million 2024 investment.

Council asked about staff support hours for newly housed individuals, the Mental Health Partners acute care campus, shelter bed utilization averaging about 10 unused beds per night, and whether a council seat on the Homeless Solutions Committee is possible. Questions also covered the evidence for sanctioned encampments and the funding for new services. Staff agreed to provide data on shelter bed usage, family homelessness and shelter capacity trends.

Staff presented options for alternative sheltering, including safe outdoor spaces and pallet shelters, with cost estimates based largely on Denver and noting that infrastructure and staffing drive costs. Council members expressed interest in further exploration, with some preferring incremental shelter bed expansion or indoor options.
